comments.author: sblom
comments.story_title: A Programming Language, now in HTML (50th anniversary)
comments.why_zh: 展示 APL 在生命游戏中的优雅力量。
comments.text_zh: 对某些东西来说，它有着令人难以置信的优雅力量（想立刻爱上它就看看 [VIDEO]）。但我发现，想用它做大多数事情根本不值得。每次我不得不从它的数组编程核心逃到更熟悉的流控制结构——那些只在后来版本的 APL 里才出现的东西——我都觉得像在作弊。我觉得它很适合当谜题语言（也就是说，乐趣来自琢磨_怎么_把话说出来，而不是单纯把事做完），但不幸的是，想搞懂别人写的代码怎么工作，就更像在解谜了。补充完整背景：我用 J 的时间比用 APL 本身还多。
comments.text: It has an incredible amount of elegant power for some things (see [VIDEO] if you want to immediately fall in love). But I've found that trying to use it for most things just isn't worthwhile. It feels like cheating every time I have to escape from its array programming core to the more familiar flow control structures that only came along in later versions of APL. I think it makes a good puzzle language (i.e. the fun comes from figuring out _how_ to say something rather that just raw getting stuff done), but unfortunately, it's even more of a puzzle to figure out how code that someone else wrote works. For full context: I've spent more time using J than APL itself.

comments.author: kragen
comments.story_title: Loopless Programming
comments.why_zh: 用短视频展示数组语言为何思维方式不同。
comments.quote_zh: 试着看看这个视频；只会花你 8 分钟
comments.text_zh: 试着看看这个视频；只会花你 8 分钟，但 3 分钟之内你就应该能明白，为什么数组语言不同于在 Rust 里有一个可用的 ndarray 库，或是在 Haskell 里有 typeclasses：[VIDEO]。看完之后，你当然会怀疑 APL 和其他数组语言（比如 J）是某种用于数值线性代数之类事情的 DSL，而 Numpy 和 Octave 当然就是干这个的。（尽管 Game of Life 不是线性代数，但它显然是基于矩阵的，所以看起来也没差那么远。）Dyalog 还发布过一些其他视频，演示他们专有的 APL 用于不同用途，但我觉得更有趣的一个是 [LINK]，作者是 J 的发明者 Roger Hui。这个视频有一个半小时，但它展示了一些把不同问题归约为多维数组的方法，有些情况下是指针（“boxes”）的多维数组。这应该足以让你相信，这里有一种异类式的思维方式，与 Haskell 和 Rust 的方法相当不同，而且可以应用于各种各样的问题。不过，我不是 Stevan Apter，所以我不会试图说服你这种异类式思维更好。但它显然不同，而不同的思维方式在不同情境下效果最好。
comments.text: Try watching this video; it will only take you 8 minutes, but within 3 minutes you should have an idea of why array languages are different from having an ndarray library available in Rust or having typeclasses in Haskell: [VIDEO] After you watch that you will of course suspect that APL and other array languages like J are a sort of DSL for things like numerical linear algebra, which is of course what Numpy and Octave are. (Even though the Game of Life isn't linear algebra, it's very clearly matrix-based, so it doesn't seem that far off.) Dyalog has posted some other videos demonstrating the use of their proprietary APL for different things, but I think a more interesting one is [LINK] , by J inventor Roger Hui. This is an hour and a half, but it demonstrates some approaches to reducing different problems to multidimensional arrays, of pointers ("boxes") in some cases. This ought to be enough to convince you that there's an alien kind of thinking here, quite different from the Haskell and Rust approaches, that can be applied to a wide variety of problems. Now, I'm not Stevan Apter, so I'm not going to try to convince you that this alien kind of thinking is better . But it's clearly different , and different ways of thinking work best in different situations.

comments.text_zh:
那你会更喜欢这样的 numpy 写法吗？

def life(x):
    y = np.array([np.roll(x, -1), np.roll(x, 0),np.roll(x, 1)])
    y = np.array([np.roll(y, -1, 1), np.roll(y, 0, 1),np.roll(y, 1, 1)])
    z = y.sum(1).sum(0)
    a = np.array([3 == z, 4==z])
    c = np.logical_and(np.array([np.ones(x.shape), x]), a)
    return np.logical_or(c[0], c[1])
